widget.prompt: What makes a shape a quadrilateral?

options.label: Exactly 4 straight sides, closed up
options.feedback: Quad = four. Any closed shape with four straight sides qualifies — squares, kites, lopsided ones too.

options.label: Four EQUAL sides
options.feedback: Equal isn't required — a long thin rectangle is a quadrilateral with unequal sides. Four straight sides is the whole test.

options.label: Four curved sides
options.feedback: The sides must be straight — curves disqualify. (A circle has no straight sides at all.)

options.label: Three corners
options.feedback: Three corners makes a triangle. Four sides always brings four corners along.

explanationVariants: A quadrilateral is any closed shape with exactly four straight sides — equal or not.
The family is huge: squares, rectangles, rhombuses, trapezoids, and every lopsided four-sider.

widget.prompt: A rectangle is 8 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its perimeter?

commonErrors.feedback: 11 walked only TWO sides (8 + 3) — the fence goes all the way around: two 8s and two 3s.
24 multiplied 8 × 3 — that's the AREA, the grass inside. Perimeter walks the fence: add all four sides.

hints: Perimeter = the walk around the edge.
A rectangle has TWO lengths and TWO widths.
explanationVariants: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22 cm — every side gets walked.
Shortcut: (8 + 3) doubled, because the sides come in pairs.

widget.prompt: A rectangle is covered by 4 rows of 6 unit squares. What is its area in square units?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 added 4 + 6 — that's edge-thinking. Area COUNTS the squares: 4 equal rows of 6.
20 is the PERIMETER (4+6 doubled) — the fence, not the carpet. The squares inside count 4 × 6.

explanationVariants: 4 rows × 6 squares = 24 square units — area is multiplication you can see.
Skip-count the rows: 6, 12, 18, 24.

widget.prompt: Is a square also a rectangle?

options.label: Yes — it has 4 right angles with opposite sides equal, plus a bonus: ALL sides equal
options.feedback: A square passes every rectangle test, so it's a rectangle — the extra-special kind.

options.label: No — squares and rectangles are different shapes
options.feedback: Run the rectangle checklist on a square: four right angles ✓, opposite sides equal ✓. It passes — squares are special members of the rectangle family.

options.label: Only large squares are
options.feedback: Size never changes a shape's family — a tiny square and a huge one pass the same tests.

options.label: Only if you tilt it
options.feedback: Tilting changes nothing about sides and angles — family membership survives every turn.

hints: Does a square meet every one?
explanationVariants: Every square is a rectangle — it meets all the requirements and adds one more (equal sides).
Family logic: the special member belongs to the general family, not the other way around.

widget.prompt: A square has sides of 7 cm. What is its perimeter?

commonErrors.feedback: 14 walked two sides. A square's fence has FOUR equal stretches: 7, four times.
49 is 7 × 7 — the area inside. The perimeter adds the four 7-cm sides.

explanationVariants: 4 × 7 = 28 cm of fence.
Perimeter of any square is just 4 × side — equal sides make it one multiplication.

widget.prompt: Which shape has exactly 6 sides?

options.label: Hexagon
options.feedback: Hex = six — six sides, six corners, like a honeycomb cell.

options.label: Pentagon
options.feedback: Penta = five. One side short of six.

options.label: Octagon
options.feedback: Octo = eight, like an octopus's arms — two sides too many.

options.label: Triangle
options.feedback: Tri = three — half of six.

hints: Hex, penta, octo, tri — which means six?
explanationVariants: Hexagon: hex = six sides — the honeycomb shape.
Shape names are counting words in disguise: tri 3, quad 4, penta 5, hex 6, octo 8.

widget.prompt: A rectangle's perimeter is 20 cm, and one side is 6 cm. How long is the side NEXT to it?

commonErrors.feedback: 14 took one 6 off the 20 — but the rectangle has TWO 6-cm sides in its fence.
8 is what's left after removing both 6s (20 − 12) — but that 8 covers BOTH remaining sides. Each one is half of it.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Remove both 6s from the fence, then split what's left between the two equal sides.

hints: The fence holds two 6s and two mystery sides.
That leftover covers TWO equal sides.
explanationVariants: 20 − 6 − 6 = 8, split between two sides: 4 cm each.
Check the fence: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 ✓.

widget.prompt: Which of these is a RIGHT angle?

options.label: A square corner, like the corner of a book
options.feedback: Right angle = square corner — the L-shape a book cover makes.

options.label: Any sharp, pointy corner
options.feedback: Pointier than square is a SMALLER angle (acute). Right means exactly square.

options.label: A corner opened wider than a square's
options.feedback: Wider than square is a bigger angle (obtuse) — past the right-angle mark.

options.label: Only corners that point to the right
options.feedback: 'Right' names the SHAPE of the corner, not a direction — a square corner aimed any way is still a right angle.

hints: Find a book or paper corner.
That exact openness is the standard.
explanationVariants: A right angle is a perfect square corner — test with any book's corner.
The name is old language for 'upright,' not the direction right.

widget.prompt: How many vertices (corners) does a pentagon have?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 belongs to the hexagon. A pentagon's five sides meet at exactly five corners.
4 corners is a quadrilateral. Penta = five — and sides and corners always match.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Sides and vertices come in equal counts.

hints: Each pair of neighboring sides meets at one corner.
explanationVariants: A pentagon has 5 vertices — every closed shape has as many corners as sides.
Walk the edge: each turn you make is one vertex, and you turn once per side.

widget.prompt: Sort each shape: quadrilateral or not?

items.label: Square
items.feedback: Four straight sides — the tidiest member of the family.

items.label: Trapezoid
items.feedback: Lopsided but legal: four straight sides is the only test.

items.label: Triangle
items.feedback: Three sides — one short. Tri, not quad.

items.label: Circle
items.feedback: A circle has zero straight sides — none of the four the club requires.

widget.missFeedback: Count straight sides: exactly four passes, anything else fails.
widget.successFeedback: Square and trapezoid are in; triangle (3 sides) and circle (0 straight sides) are out.

explanationVariants: The quadrilateral club has one rule: four straight sides — neatness optional.
Trapezoids prove it: uneven, unparallel-mostly, and still fully quadrilateral.

widget.prompt: A garden is 5 meters by 5 meters. What is its area in square meters?

commonErrors.feedback: 20 is the fence (perimeter). The area counts the square meters of soil inside: 5 rows of 5.
10 added the two sides. Area fills the space: 5 × 5.

explanationVariants: 5 × 5 = 25 square meters of garden.
Fence vs soil: the perimeter is 20 m of edge; the area is 25 squares of ground.

widget.prompt: A rectangle is split into 4 EQUAL parts. What is the area of each part?

options.label: 1/4 of the whole rectangle's area
options.feedback: Equal parts share the area evenly — four parts, each a quarter of it.

options.label: 4 whole rectangles
options.feedback: Splitting never grows the shape — the parts together still make ONE rectangle.

options.label: It depends which part you pick
options.feedback: EQUAL parts is the given — every part carries exactly the same area.

options.label: 1/2 of the area
options.feedback: A half would mean only two parts. Four equal parts cut the area into fourths.

hints: The parts are equal by promise.
Four equal shares of one area.
explanationVariants: Four equal parts → each holds 1/4 of the area — fractions ARE geometry here.
The parts may look different in shape, but equal cutting guarantees equal area.

widget.prompt: A rectangle is 9 cm by 2 cm. What is its area?

commonErrors.feedback: 22 is the perimeter — the walk around. The inside holds 2 rows of 9 squares.
11 added the sides. Area multiplies them: 9 × 2.

explanationVariants: 9 × 2 = 18 square cm.
The flip works here too: 2 rows of 9 or 9 columns of 2 — same 18 squares.

widget.prompt: A shape has 4 equal sides but NO right angles. What is it?

options.label: A rhombus
options.feedback: Four equal sides is the rhombus test — right angles aren't required. It's a square that leaned over.

options.label: A square
options.feedback: So close — but a square needs BOTH: equal sides AND right angles. Missing the angles, it's a rhombus.

options.label: A rectangle
options.feedback: A rectangle needs the right angles this shape lacks (and allows unequal side pairs).

options.label: A triangle
options.feedback: Four sides rules out triangles entirely — this is a quadrilateral question.

hints: Which name needs only the sides?
explanationVariants: Equal sides without right angles = rhombus — the leaning square.
Add right angles to a rhombus and it straightens into a square.

widget.prompt: A floor is covered by 3 rows of 8 tiles. How many tiles cover it?

commonErrors.feedback: 11 added 3 + 8. The rows are equal groups — three groups of eight tiles.
38 glued the digits. Count a row (8), three times.

explanationVariants: 3 × 8 = 24 tiles — area counting IS multiplication.
This is why area formulas work: rows of unit squares are equal groups.

widget.prompt: Two shapes have the SAME perimeter. Must they have the same area?

options.label: No — a 1-by-5 rectangle and a 3-by-3 square both have perimeter 12, but areas 5 and 9
options.feedback: Same fence length can wrap very different amounts of grass — skinny shapes waste fence.

options.label: Yes — same perimeter forces same area
options.feedback: Test it: 1×5 (fence 12, grass 5) vs 3×3 (fence 12, grass 9). Same walk, different fields.

options.label: Only if both are squares
options.feedback: Two same-perimeter squares DO match areas — but the question covers all shapes, and skinny ones break the pattern.

options.label: Perimeter and area are the same measurement
options.feedback: They answer different questions: perimeter walks the border; area counts the inside.

hints: Try building two shapes with fence 12.
explanationVariants: Perimeter 12 fits both a 1×5 (area 5) and a 3×3 (area 9) — fence length doesn't fix the grass.
The squarer the shape, the more area a fixed fence holds — skinny rectangles are wasteful.

widget.prompt: A hexagon has all sides 4 cm long. What is its perimeter?

commonErrors.feedback: 16 walked only four sides — quadrilateral habit! A hexagon's fence has SIX stretches.
10 added 4 + 6 (side length + side count). The fence repeats the 4, six times: multiply.

explanationVariants: 6 × 4 = 24 cm around the hexagon.
Equal-sided perimeters are always side-count × side-length.

widget.prompt: Which is true of every rectangle?

options.label: Opposite sides are parallel and equal
options.feedback: The rectangle's signature: two matched pairs of parallel sides, corners all square.

options.label: All four sides are equal
options.feedback: That's the SQUARE — the one special rectangle. Most rectangles pair a long side with a short one.

options.label: It has 5 corners
options.feedback: Four sides bring exactly four corners — five corners is a pentagon's business.

options.label: It must be wider than it is tall
options.feedback: Turn it sideways — still a rectangle! Orientation never changes what a shape IS.

hints: Long ones, tall ones, square ones…
explanationVariants: Every rectangle: opposite sides parallel and equal, four right angles — tall, wide, or square.
The orientation trap: shapes keep their names at every angle.

widget.prompt: A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, and 10 cm. What is its perimeter?

commonErrors.feedback: 48 multiplied 6 × 8 — the area reflex. Perimeter is a WALK: add every side.
14 walked only two sides (6 + 8) — the 10-cm side completes the loop.

explanationVariants: 6 + 8 + 10 = 24 cm around the triangle.
Friendly order: 6 + 8 = 14, then 14 + 10 = 24 — or spot the 6 + 10 + 8 = 16 + 8 route.

widget.prompt: A shape is cut into 6 equal pieces. Each piece is what fraction of the shape's AREA?

options.feedback: Six equal shares of one area — each is a sixth of it.
6/1 would be six whole shapes! Each PIECE is small: one of the six.
Count all the pieces for the bottom number — the cut made six.

options.label: Impossible to know without measuring
options.feedback: EQUAL is the key word — equal pieces of one whole must each be 1/6, no ruler needed.

hints: The pieces are equal by promise.
How many pieces share the area?
explanationVariants: Six equal pieces → each is 1/6 of the area — the fraction facts apply to space itself.
Equal-area pieces can even be different SHAPES — the fraction cares only about area.

widget.prompt: How many unit squares cover a 7-by-3 rectangle?

commonErrors.feedback: 20 is the perimeter (7 + 3 doubled) — the border. The covering counts 3 rows of 7.
10 added the side lengths. Covering fills rows: 7 × 3.

explanationVariants: 7 × 3 = 21 unit squares.
Skip-count rows: 7, 14, 21.

problems.body: A riddle with one parallel pair.

widget.prompt: I have 4 sides, and exactly ONE pair of my sides is parallel. What am I?

options.label: A trapezoid
options.feedback: One parallel pair is the trapezoid's calling card.

options.label: A parallelogram
options.feedback: Parallelograms have TWO parallel pairs — one pair too many for this riddle.

options.label: A square
options.feedback: Squares carry two parallel pairs (plus equal sides and right angles) — far too fancy.

options.label: A pentagon
options.feedback: Five sides — this riddle's shape has four.

hints: Four sides narrows it to quadrilaterals.
explanationVariants: Exactly one parallel pair = trapezoid.
The parallel-pair count sorts the family: two pairs → parallelogram branch; one pair → trapezoid.

widget.prompt: A square's perimeter is 36 cm. How long is ONE side?

commonErrors.feedback: 32 subtracted 4 from 36 — but the fence isn't 4 cm longer than a side; it's 4 sides LONG. Split 36 into four.
18 halved the fence — that's two sides' worth. A square's fence splits FOUR ways.

explanationVariants: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm per side.
Check: 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 36 ✓ — the fence rebuilds.

widget.prompt: Build the AREA of a 6-by-4 rectangle.

commonBuilds.feedback: 6 + 4 is edge-thinking — half the perimeter. Area counts ROWS of squares: 4 rows of 6, which multiplies.

widget.successFeedback: 6 × 4 = 24 square units — rows of unit squares are equal groups.

explanationVariants: Area of a 6-by-4 rectangle: 6 × 4 = 24 square units.
The flip 4 × 6 builds the same carpet — rows become columns.

widget.prompt: Which shape can tile a floor with NO gaps and NO overlaps?

options.label: Squares
options.feedback: Squares snap edge-to-edge perfectly — that's why tiles and grids love them.

options.label: Circles
options.feedback: Circles always leave little curved gaps between neighbors — no flat edges to share.

options.label: No flat shape can
options.feedback: Plenty can! Squares, rectangles, even triangles and hexagons tile perfectly — bathroom floors prove it daily.

options.label: Only very large shapes
options.feedback: Size doesn't fix gaps — a shape's EDGES decide whether it locks together.

explanationVariants: Squares tile perfectly — full edges pressed to full edges, no gaps.
That gap-free locking is exactly why we measure area in SQUARE units.

widget.prompt: A rectangular pen is 12 m by 5 m. How much fencing goes all the way around?

commonErrors.feedback: 60 is 12 × 5 — the AREA of grass inside. Fencing follows the border: add all four sides.
17 fenced only two sides (12 + 5). The pen needs both pairs: 12 + 5 + 12 + 5.

explanationVariants: Pair shortcut: 12 + 5 = 17, doubled to 34.

widget.prompt: A rectangle is halved two ways: into two TALL strips, or into two WIDE strips. Compare one tall strip's area to one wide strip's.

options.label: Equal — each is 1/2 of the same rectangle
options.feedback: Different shapes, same share: half the area is half the area, however you slice it.

options.label: The tall strip is bigger
options.feedback: Both cuts split the SAME rectangle into two equal parts — each part is exactly half.

options.label: The wide strip is bigger
options.feedback: Wide or tall, each strip holds half the squares of the same whole.

options.label: You can't compare different shapes
options.feedback: Areas compare fine across shapes — count the unit squares: both strips hold the same count.

hints: Both cuts halve the SAME whole.
Half of equal wholes are equal.
explanationVariants: Both strips are 1/2 of the same rectangle — equal areas wearing different shapes.
Cut a 4×6: tall strips are 2×6 = 12; wide strips are 4×3 = 12. Same twelve squares.

widget.prompt: Two triangles and one square: how many sides in ALL?

commonErrors.feedback: 7 counted ONE triangle plus the square — the second triangle brings three more.
12 counted two squares' worth somewhere — triangles carry 3 sides each, not 4.

explanationVariants: 3 + 3 + 4 = 10 sides in the pile.
Groups view: 2 × 3 + 4 = 10.

widget.prompt: Every square is also a rhombus because…

options.label: …it has four equal sides — the only rhombus requirement
options.feedback: The rhombus test asks one thing: equal sides. Squares pass, with bonus right angles.

options.label: …actually, it isn't one
options.feedback: Run the test: four equal sides? A square says yes. Extra features never disqualify.

options.label: …squares are small
options.feedback: Size sits outside every shape test — families are about sides and angles.

options.label: …all rhombuses are squares
options.feedback: Backwards! A leaning rhombus fails the square's right-angle test. Squares are the special rhombuses, not the reverse.

hints: What is the rhombus's one requirement?
explanationVariants: Squares pass the rhombus test (four equal sides) — they're rhombuses with right angles.
Family arrows point one way: every square is a rhombus; only upright rhombuses are squares.

widget.prompt: A rug is 4 m by 6 m. The room is 5 m by 8 m. How many square meters of floor are NOT covered by the rug?

commonErrors.feedback: 24 is the RUG's area — the covered part. The bare floor is the room minus the rug.
40 is the whole ROOM. Subtract the rug's 24 to find the bare part.
64 ADDED the two areas. The rug lies INSIDE the room — subtract it.

explanationVariants: Room 40 − rug 24 = 16 square meters bare.
Guard the sizes: the bare part must be smaller than the whole room — 16 fits; 64 can't.
